deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the end of §6 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published by Dedekind 1867). The section deals with improper integrals ∫_0^a f(x) dx where f becomes infinite at the single point x=0. The page finishes the logarithmic-scale criteria begun on the previous page, adds a remark on oscillating integrands, and then turns to the main problem.

Notation. Write L_1(x)=log(1/x) and L_{k+1}=log L_k. Riemann writes log^k(1/x) for the k-fold iterated logarithm, not for a power.

(1) Differentials (implicit step, mine).
- dL_1 = -dx/x.
- In general dL_{k+1} = dL_k / L_k = -dx/(x L_1 ⋯ L_k).
- Hence f(x)·x·L_1⋯L_n = f(x)dx / (-dL_{n+1}). This is the identity on the first line, continuing x f = f dx/(-dL_1) and x L_1 f = f dx/(-dL_2) from the previous page.

(2) Necessary condition.
- Suppose F_n(x) := x L_1⋯L_n f(x) > C > 0 for 0 < x < a.
- Then ∫_x^a f dt > C ∫_x^a (-dL_{n+1}) = C (L_{n+1}(x) - L_{n+1}(a)).
- The right side tends to ∞ as x→0+.
- So if the integral converges, F_n cannot stay above a positive constant (nor, symmetrically, below a negative one).
- If F_n has only finitely many maxima and minima near 0, it is eventually monotone and so has a limit. That limit must then be 0. Here 'sie' refers to these product functions, as 'diese Function' did on the previous page.

(3) Sufficient condition.
- d(L_n^{1-α}) = (1-α) L_n^{-α} dL_n = -(1-α) dx / (x L_1⋯L_{n-1} L_n^α).
- Hence f · x L_1⋯L_{n-1} L_n^α = f dx (1-α) / (-d L_n^{1-α}).
- For α>1 the comparison integral ∫_0 dx/(x L_1⋯L_{n-1} L_n^α) = [L_n^{1-α}/(α-1)] converges, since L_n^{1-α} → 0.
- So if this product → 0, then |f| ≤ ε·(comparison integrand) near 0, and ∫ f dx converges (absolutely) as the lower limit → 0.
- Together these give the Abel/Bertrand-type logarithmic scale for the order of infinity of an integrable singularity.

(4) Oscillating integrands.
- If f has infinitely many maxima and minima near 0, nothing can be said about the order of its infinity.
- Given |f| (which alone determines the order), one can always choose signs so that ∫ f converges. Implicitly: alternate signs on successive intervals so that the partial integrals cancel and their tails shrink.
- Example: g(x) = x cos(e^{1/x}). Then g'(x) = cos(e^{1/x}) + (1/x) e^{1/x} sin(e^{1/x}).
- ∫_ε^a g' = g(a) - g(ε) → g(a) because |g(ε)| ≤ ε. So the improper integral converges.
- Yet |g'| reaches size ~ e^{1/x}/x near 0, i.e. infinite order relative to the unit 1/x.

(5) Transition. 'Enough on this subject, which really belongs to another area'; the text now turns to the general investigation of representability by a trigonometric series (§7 on the next page).
errors: No mathematical errors found. The derivative of x cos(e^{1/x}) is correct, and both differential identities check.

Step (2) is valid only because the hypothesis 'no infinitely many maxima/minima' is applied to the product function F_n itself, which makes F_n eventually monotone. If it were applied to f, the conclusion F_n→0 for n≥1 would not follow: monotone f with convergent integral does not force x log(1/x) f(x)→0, by analogy with Olivier's theorem for series.
The sign-choice claim in (4) is stated without proof. It tacitly assumes |f| is integrable on every [ε,a].
'Unendlich wird' for the example means 'unbounded near 0'. The function oscillates and does not tend to ∞; the convergence is only conditional.

results.what: Logarithmic scale of necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence of an improper integral at a singular point: x L1⋯Ln f → 0 necessary (for eventually monotone products); x L1⋯L_{n-1} L_n^α f → 0 with α>1 sufficient
results.modern_name: Abel–Bertrand (de Morgan–Bertrand) logarithmic scale / comparison test for improper integrals
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (1827, posthumous), de Morgan (1839), Bertrand (1842), Bonnet; Cauchy-type comparison

results.what: Oscillating integrand with unbounded growth of infinite order whose improper integral converges: d/dx[x cos(e^{1/x})]
results.modern_name: Conditionally convergent improper Riemann integral; Riemann's example of an integrable singularity of infinite order

results.what: Remark that for functions with infinitely many oscillations, convergence of the integral imposes no restriction on the order of infinity of |f|
results.modern_name: Conditional vs absolute convergence of improper integrals

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift (§6, end), and the cos(e^{1/x}) example is well known as his. Nothing is unpublished or unexpected.

transcription_corrections: 'log^n' here denotes the n-fold iterated logarithm, not a power; the transcription is otherwise faithful to the image.
